512.title: What does go
512.hook: the Name and good deeds go along (Sukhmani 19)
512.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting the nineteenth ashtpadi of Sukhmani Sahib hear that only the Name, earned through practice, goes along at the end; many sum up Guru Nanak's way as remembering the Name, honest work and sharing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dasvandh: if even a needle stays behind, you choose where your wealth lands. Today the nineteenth ashtpadi answers the obvious next question.

At the airport check-in desk there's a scale, and a number on a sign: fifty pounds. Anything over that costs you, or stays home. So people kneel on the floor of the terminal, unzipping suitcases, pulling out the extra shoes, the heavy book, the jar of pickle from an aunt. It's a strange little moment of truth. What actually matters enough to carry? Sukhmani's nineteenth ashtpadi has its own scale, and its own short list.
screen: `THE SCALE AT CHECK-IN.` → `WHAT MATTERS ENOUGH TO CARRY?` → `WHAT DOES GO.`

segments.voice: Go back two days, to the salok that opens the nineteenth ashtpadi. Its first line said nothing goes along without devotion. Its second line already holds today's answer: earn the Name of the Lord, says Nanak; this is the wealth worth having. The verb is kamaavanaa, to earn: the ordinary Punjabi word for earning a living, a day's wages. So the Name isn't pictured as a lottery ticket. It's earned the way bread is earned, by showing up, again and again, over years. And it's the one kind of savings the scale at the end can't weigh out. Then there's a second thing that travels: what you've done. Sikhs hear this in the closing salok of Japji, the morning prayer: by their own deeds, some come near and some go far. Guru Nanak's teaching is often summed up in three short phrases: remember the Name, earn honestly, and share what you have. Two of the three are about how you treat other people. Read that way, the soul doesn't carry a trophy shelf or a bank balance. It carries a character: what it became through the remembering and the giving. Kindness done isn't a thing you own; it's something you've turned into. That's why it fits in the bag. And there's a quiet comfort in that. You can't take the house or the title. But the part of you that learned to be generous? Read with Japji's closing line, that's the part that comes along.
screen: `THE SALOK: NOTHING ELSE GOES ALONG.` · `KAMAAVANAA: EARN IT LIKE WAGES.` · `YOUR DEEDS BRING YOU NEAR OR FAR.` · `YOU CARRY WHAT YOU BECAME.` · then, large: `KINDNESS TRAVELS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who could use something real from you, something that will still be true next month: an hour, a skill, a long-overdue apology, a regular phone call. Picture yourself doing it, all the way through, and see the first small step. If you pray, rest in Waheguru between breaths.
Karmee, by deeds: in Sukhmani's nineteenth ashtpadi only the earned Name goes along, and in Sikh teaching karmee, our deeds, bring us near or far.
Your line: kindness travels. You carry what you became, not what you owned. See you tomorrow.

513.title: Living ashtpadi 19
513.howItsDone: Sikh teaching honors the householder's life, grihasti, and Guru Nanak's picture of the lotus untouched by the water is used for living in the world without being owned by it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, karmee: by deeds we come near or far, and kindness is the part that travels. Today we take the whole nineteenth ashtpadi off the page and into the house.

Every home has one. The drawer. Dead batteries, a takeout menu from a restaurant that closed, three keys to locks nobody remembers, a charger for a phone long gone. Nobody decided to keep any of it. It just collected, the way things do when nobody's looking. And every time you open that drawer looking for scissors, you have to dig. The nineteenth ashtpadi has spent three days on what stays behind and what goes along. Living it starts somewhere very small. Maybe with that drawer.
screen: `THE DRAWER EVERY HOME HAS.` → `IT JUST COLLECTED.` → `LIVING IT STARTS SMALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the nineteenth ashtpadi in one breath: the riches, youth and power we pile up stay behind; the Name we earn and the good we do go along. So how do people actually live that? Not, in Sikh teaching, by leaving home. Guru Nanak spent his last years farming at Kartarpur, raising a family, running a community kitchen. Sikhs call that life grihasti, the householder's path, and hold it up as a full spiritual life. So living light doesn't mean owning nothing. It means owning lightly, holding things with an open hand. Guru Nanak gave a picture for it in the Sidh Gosht, his conversation with the Siddhas, the yogi masters. In paraphrase: as the lotus floats on the water and stays untouched by it, as the duck swims the stream and stays dry. Kamal, the lotus: it lives in the pond and isn't soaked by it. In the world, not drowned in it. And then there's the drawer. It may seem silly to link a junk drawer to a hymn, but Sukhmani works on the mind, and the mind is often cluttered in exactly that way: old grudges, worries about things that never happened, plans for a life you outgrew. Clearing a drawer won't clear all that. But it's practice. You learn to look at something, admit you're not using it, and let it go to someone who will. That's living light: not empty hands, open ones.
screen: `STAYS BEHIND, GOES ALONG.` · `NOT RUNNING AWAY: THE HOUSEHOLDER.` · `THE LOTUS: IN THE WATER, NOT SOAKED.` · `THE DRAWER: PRACTICE LETTING GO.` · then, large: `OPEN HANDS, NOT EMPTY ONES.`

segments.voice: Go to the drawer if you can, or picture it clearly, and take out one thing at a time, holding each for a breath: do I use this, could someone else? Make three small piles, keep, give, throw away, without hurrying and without judging yourself for what's in there. If you pray, say Waheguru as each thing goes.
Kamal, the lotus: the householder's way is owning lightly, like the kamal on the water, untouched by it, and letting go of what you don't use so it can move on.
Your line: live light. The lotus lives in the pond and stays dry. Day five hundred thirteen.

514.title: Ashtpadi 20, salok: wandering, I came
514.hook: phirat phirat: wandering and wandering, I have come to Your refuge (Sukhmani 20)
514.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twentieth ashtpadi begin with its salok, in which the seeker, after long wandering, comes to God's refuge and asks only to be joined to devotion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kamal: the lotus that lives in the water and stays untouched. Today a new ashtpadi begins, the twentieth, with a traveler who finally stops.

Phirat phirat. Say it out loud and it sounds like footsteps: phirat, phirat, phirat. It's the first word of the twentieth ashtpadi, and it means wandering, turning, going round and round. A car circles a city at night, looking for an address. Left, then left again, back past the same gas station, the phone saying recalculating. And then, finally, the right door, the porch light on, and someone saying come in. Today's salok is that moment of arrival.
screen: `PHIRAT, PHIRAT: LIKE FOOTSTEPS.` → `RECALCULATING.` → `THE PORCH LIGHT ON.`

segments.voice: The salok has two lines. In paraphrase: wandering and wandering, O God, I have come, and fallen at Your sanctuary. This is Nanak's prayer, O God: attach me to Your devotion. Start with the repeated word. Gurbani often doubles a word to make it last: phirat phirat isn't one detour, it's a whole life of them. Some readers hear in it the long round of births and deaths, the soul turning through lifetime after lifetime. Others hear the ordinary wandering of a single life: job to job, want to want, one more thing that was supposed to finally make it feel settled. The text holds both. Then the verb: aaiaa, I have come. Not I have earned my way in, or I have found the answer. Just: I'm here. Then pariaa: I've fallen, or laid myself down, at Your saran, Your refuge. It's the posture of someone too tired to keep standing. The last line is the request, and notice what it doesn't ask for: no proof the wandering was worth it, no prize at the end. It asks: attach me to Your bhagti, Your devotion. Keep me here. After nineteen ashtpadis of lists and pictures and warnings, the twentieth opens with no argument at all. Just a traveler at the door, and a request to stay.
screen: `THE SALOK: I HAVE COME, I HAVE FALLEN.` · `PHIRAT PHIRAT: A WHOLE LIFE OF DETOURS.` · `NOT EARNED, JUST ARRIVED.` · `THE REQUEST: KEEP ME HERE.` · then, large: `I HAVE COME.`

segments.voice: Let yourself arrive where you are: feel your body settle into the chair or the floor as if you'd just walked a long way, and let the shoulders drop. With each breath out, say silently, I have come, and when thoughts start wandering, notice the footsteps, phirat phirat, and come back. If you pray, rest in Waheguru.
Phirat, wandering, going round and round: its salok, phirat phirat, the seeker arrives after long wandering at God's refuge and asks only to be kept in devotion.
Your line: I have come. No prize asked for, only to be kept near. Rest easy.

515.title: A beggar at the door
515.hook: the soul stands like a beggar at the Lord's door (Sukhmani 20)
515.carry: the dust of good people's feet
515.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting the twentieth ashtpadi of Sukhmani Sahib take the posture of the jaachak, the beggar, asking God for the Name and for the dust of the feet of the holy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, phirat: the long wandering, and a traveler who finally arrives at the door. Today we hear what the traveler says, standing there.

Some people will carry a couch up four flights alone rather than text a friend. Some will sit up until midnight with a form they don't understand rather than ask the coworker who does. Asking is hard. It means admitting you can't do it yourself, and it means someone might say no. So it's striking that the first stanza of the twentieth ashtpadi doesn't open with a king, or a scholar, or a saint. It opens with a jaachak: a beggar, standing at the door, asking.
screen: `A COUCH, FOUR FLIGHTS, ALONE.` → `ASKING IS HARD.` → `JAACHAK: THE ONE WHO ASKS.`

segments.voice: The stanza opens, in paraphrase: the humble beggar begs God for a gift. In Your mercy, give me Your Name. Then a second request: I ask for the dust of the feet of the holy. Jaachak is a beggar, one who asks for alms; jaachai is the verb, to beg. Guru Arjan sets them side by side, the beggar begging, so you can't miss the posture. It's an old picture in Indian devotion, and Gurbani returns to it often: the soul at God's door with an empty bowl. Here's what's surprising: the beggar isn't ashamed. In Sikh thought the real trouble is haumai, the inflated self that insists it needs no one. A beggar has already let that go. They know the bowl is empty and aren't pretending otherwise. That honesty is the opening. And look at what the beggar asks for. Not money, not success, not a long life. The Name, and the dust of good people's feet. That second request sounds odd to modern ears. It's an image of deep humility: to be so low before good people that you'd count the dust they walk in as a gift. Sikhs echo it when they bow, touch the floor, or serve shoes at the gurdwara door. Yesterday the traveler stood at God's door. Today the traveler finds the words, and they turn out to be a beggar's words.
screen: `JAACHAK JAACHAI: THE BEGGAR BEGS.` · `NO SHAME: THE BOWL IS EMPTY.` · `THE ASK: THE NAME, AND THE DUST.` · `THE TRAVELER FINDS THE WORDS.` · then, large: `A BEGGAR AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands open on your knees, palms up like a bowl, and let one real need come to mind, something you've been trying to handle alone, without dressing it up. If you pray, hold it in your open hands and ask, the way the beggar asks; if you don't, simply notice who you could ask: a friend, a colleague, a neighbor.
Jaachak, a beggar, one who asks for alms: in Sukhmani's twentieth ashtpadi the jaachak asks God for the Name and for the dust of good people's feet.
Your line: the dust of good people's feet. Asking isn't shameful; it's honest about the empty bowl. Day five hundred fifteen.

516.title: Mercy asked for
516.hook: the prayer asks for mercy, not reward (Sukhmani 20)
516.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twentieth ashtpadi ask for the Name with the words kar kirpaa, in Your mercy, and Gurbani links grace received with forgiveness given.

segments.voice: Yesterday, jaachak: the beggar at God's door, asking for the Name and the dust of good people's feet. Today, the two words that came before the asking.

A loyalty card at a coffee shop. Ten stamps, and the eleventh cup is free. It's a tidy little deal: you do this, you get that. A lot of life runs like that card, and a lot of religion is imagined that way too. Pray enough, give enough, behave well enough, and eventually the reward is stamped and due. Sukhmani's twentieth ashtpadi tucks two small words into the beggar's request that tear the card in half. Kar kirpaa.
screen: `TEN STAMPS, ONE FREE CUP.` → `DO THIS, GET THAT.` → `KAR KIRPAA.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's stanza, in paraphrase: the beggar begs for a gift; in Your mercy, give me Your Name. Kar kirpaa: do mercy, show kindness. Kirpaa is grace or mercy, a gift given because the giver is kind, not because the receiver has filled a card. And the word for what's asked, daan, is a gift too: alms, charity. Nothing in that sentence is owed. Day five hundred met the same thread in Japji: actions shape a life, but grace, nadar, opens the gate. Today it's in the beggar's own mouth. Deeds matter; Sikhs are expected to work, serve, and live well. But what the beggar asks for isn't bought by them. It's given, the way a gift is given. Why does that matter on an ordinary Tuesday? Because how you think you're treated tends to become how you treat others. If everything is earned, then the people who've hurt you owe you, and the debt can feel permanent. If you've been met with mercy, the ledger loosens. There's a salok of the poet-saint Kabir, recorded in the Guru Granth Sahib, that makes the link plainly. In paraphrase: where there is forgiveness, there is God Himself. Khimaa, forgiveness, is mercy turned outward. The beggar who asks for kirpaa learns, slowly, to give some away.

segments.voice: Picture someone who hurt you in a small way, not the deepest wound, a friend who canceled, a driver who cut you off, a sibling's careless comment, and notice the ledger in your chest: they owe me. On each breath out, loosen it a little; you don't have to excuse what happened, you're simply choosing not to keep stamping the card. If you pray, say Waheguru as you let go.

517.title: Living ashtpadi 20
517.hook: refuge is a place you can return to
517.tomorrow: Ashtpadi 21, salok: when there was nothing
517.howItsDone: Sikh practice returns to God's refuge daily, sitting with the Name at amrit vela before dawn and reciting Sohila at night, and gurdwaras keep their doors and kitchens open to all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirpaa: mercy given as a gift, not stamped on a card. Today we carry the whole twentieth ashtpadi out of the book.

There's an old man in a lot of neighborhoods who has a bench. Same bench, same park, every morning, coffee in a paper cup. Nobody owns a park bench, but everyone knows it's his. Ask him why he comes and he probably wouldn't say anything grand. He'd say: it's where I sit. A refuge doesn't have to be a fortress. Sometimes it's just a place you keep coming back to, until coming back is part of who you are. That's how the twentieth ashtpadi gets lived.
screen: `THE SAME BENCH EVERY MORNING.` → `IT'S WHERE I SIT.` → `A PLACE YOU COME BACK TO.`

segments.voice: Here's the twentieth ashtpadi in brief. A traveler, after long wandering, phirat phirat, comes to God's saran, God's refuge, and falls there. Standing at the door, the traveler becomes a beggar, asking for the Name and the dust of good people's feet, and asking it as mercy, not reward. Saran is the key word. It means shelter, sanctuary, protection. In Sukhmani it's God's saran, a refuge that's God's to give. And in Sikh practice it isn't somewhere you reach once and never leave. The traveler came after wandering, and minds wander again. So refuge is something you return to. Daily. That's partly what the daily banis are for. Sikh practice sets aside the early hours, amrit vela, the ambrosial time before dawn, for sitting with the Name, and closes the day with Sohila. The days between can be loud; the refuge is there at both ends. Gurdwaras carry the same idea in stone. The Darbar Sahib in Amritsar has doors on all four sides, which Sikhs explain as open to anyone, from any direction. Gurdwaras keep a langar for whoever comes, and travelers find a meal there, and often a place to rest. And it doesn't have to be a building. For one person it's a corner of a bedroom with a small shelf. For another, a walk at dawn. The place matters less than the returning.

Saran, refuge or sanctuary: God's saran isn't reached once and left; Sikh practice returns to it daily, morning and night.
Your line: refuge. Not reached once and left, but returned to, morning and night. See you tomorrow.

518.title: Ashtpadi 21, salok: when there was nothing
518.hook: sargun nirgun nirankaar: the Formless, with and without qualities, rested in the void (Sukhmani 21)
518.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twenty-first ashtpadi begin with a salok picturing God, with and without qualities, resting in sunn, the stillness before creation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, saran: a refuge you return to, morning and night. Today Sukhmani goes back before everything.

Before a concert begins, there's a moment. The lights dim, the coughing stops, the conductor lifts the baton, and for two or three seconds a whole hall full of people holds absolutely still. It's not empty, exactly. It's full of everything that's about to happen. Some musicians say the piece really starts there, in that silence. The twenty-first ashtpadi of Sukhmani goes looking for the silence before the biggest piece of all: the moment before there was anything. Its word is sunn.
screen: `THE HALL HOLDS ITS BREATH.` → `NOT EMPTY: FULL OF WHAT'S COMING.` → `SUNN.`

segments.voice: The salok, in paraphrase: with qualities and without them, the Formless One was Himself absorbed in the stillness of the void. He made it all Himself, Nanak, and He Himself remembers it again. Three words to open, and day five hundred one already met them. Sargun: with qualities, the One you can describe, near and present in the world. Nirgun: without qualities, beyond every description. Nirankaar: the Formless. The salok says all three in one breath, and none of them cancels the others. Then sunn, which is today's word. It comes from the Sanskrit shunya, empty. But in Gurbani sunn isn't a bleak nothing. It's the deep stillness God rested in before any world existed, sunn samaadhi, absorbed in the void, the way the hall is absorbed in silence before the music. Guru Nanak describes the same scene elsewhere, in the raag Maru: for countless ages there was only darkness, no earth, no sky, only the infinite will. Gurbani doesn't try to give a date or a mechanism. It doesn't say how long, or what the stillness was like from inside. The sources are silent there, and Sukhmani is content to leave it that way. What it gives instead is a starting point for wonder: in Sukhmani's telling, before anything there was the One, at rest, and everything came out of that stillness.
screen: `SARGUN, NIRGUN, NIRANKAAR: ONE BREATH.` · `SUNN: FROM SHUNYA, EMPTY.` · `NOT A BLEAK NOTHING: GOD'S STILLNESS.` · `NO DATE, NO MECHANISM: JUST WONDER.` · then, large: `WHEN THERE WAS NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Turn off what can be turned off, and let your eyes close or rest on the floor; you don't need to empty your mind, just stop adding to it. Listen to the quiet underneath the small sounds, the fridge, the traffic, your own breath, and let it be like the hall before the music, full and still. If you pray, rest in Waheguru without saying anything at all.
Sunn. The stillness, or void, in which the Formless One rested before creation; from the root of the word for empty, but in Gurbani full of God.
Your line: when there was nothing. In Gurbani even that stillness is full of God. That's day five hundred eighteen.
